name: Transformer-XL — segment recurrence + relative positions
aka: TXL; 'Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context'

source.title: Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context
source.authors: Dai, Yang, Yang, Carbonell, Le, Salakhutdinov (CMU / Google Brain)

problem: Vanilla Transformer LMs were trained on fixed segments with no information across segments (context fragmentation) and re-computed everything for each new token at eval. First mechanism to say: the bill is *effective context length*.
idea: Cache the previous segment's hidden states per layer (stop-gradient) and let the current segment attend to them, so effective context grows with depth × segment length; make that work with a relative positional scheme (sinusoidal R_{i−j} plus learned global u, v vectors) so cached states stay position-consistent.
buys: Dependencies '80% longer than RNNs and 450% longer than vanilla Transformers'; SOTA on enwik8 / text8 / WikiText-103 / One Billion Word
Up to ~1,800× faster than vanilla at eval because states are reused rather than recomputed
Its relative-position half is a distinct branch from Shaw's (sinusoidal, not per-offset learned)
costs: A per-layer hidden-state cache (mem_len × layers × d) that must be re-projected into K/V every step — the ancestor of, not an addition to, the KV cache
Training must feed segments in document order: no free shuffling, harder data pipelines
Recurrence gives a soft, decaying context — no random access to tokens beyond cache range; four-term relative attention is costlier per layer

chatbot2k.why: plain attention with a 2K window is simpler and exact

rag32k.why: retrieval wants random access, not decaying recurrence

coding128k.why: cross-file recall needs random access to far tokens; the decaying cache cannot give it

agent1m.why: the *idea* returns as compressive/Infini-style memory; this exact form does not

pickWhen.verdict: The relative-position idea survived; the recurrence mostly did not — until Infini-attention and the delta-rule RNNs picked it up again in 2024.

name: Sparse Transformer — strided / fixed factorized patterns
aka: OpenAI Sparse Transformer; 'locally banded sparse attention'

source.title: Generating Long Sequences with Sparse Transformers

firstShipped.model: OpenAI Jukebox (factorised sparse attention; code + weights released); GPT-3 (28 May 2020) is the first language model to ship the banded/local half

problem: Images (64×64×3 = 12K tokens), raw audio and long text made the n×n score matrix the whole cost — in FLOPs and in activation memory. Sequences of tens of thousands of steps and hundreds of layers were untrainable.
idea: Factor attention into hand-designed patterns each head can compute cheaply: 'strided' (a local window plus every ℓ-th column) and 'fixed' (attend within a block plus to summary columns), so any token reaches any other in two layers at O(n√n) cost. Plus custom block-sparse kernels and attention recomputation.
buys: O(n√n) instead of O(n²), with full receptive field in two hops
SOTA density modelling on enwik8, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-64 in 2019; sequences of tens of thousands of timesteps
The banded-local idea GPT-3 actually shipped, and the ancestor of gpt-oss's alternating banded layers
costs: Static, hand-designed patterns: no content adaptivity, information must hop through summary positions
Needs custom kernels to see real speed — a dense matmul with a mask saves nothing
Speedup at ≤2K is small; wins at 8K+ — and at those lengths FlashAttention later ate most of the niche

chatbot2k.why: dense + FlashAttention is simpler and as fast

rag32k.why: only with a kernel; the pattern may miss the relevant chunk

coding128k.why: as banded layers interleaved with dense ones (GPT-3 / gpt-oss style)

agent1m.why: fixed patterns lose relevant tokens; you want content-based selection (NSA/DSA)

pickWhen.verdict: Right when you control the kernels and the data has structure (images, audio); as a general LLM trick it survives only as the banded half of a hybrid.

secondary.label: GPT-3: 'alternating dense and locally banded sparse attention patterns … similar to the Sparse Transformer'

name: T5 relative position bias

source.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
source.authors: Raffel, Shazeer, Roberts, Lee, Narang, Matena, Zhou, Li, Liu (Google)

firstShipped.model: T5 (released with the paper); mT5, Flan-T5, UL2

problem: Keep Shaw's relative-position benefit without per-offset vectors and their O(n²d) memory, in a model meant to scale to 11B.
idea: Each relative offset adds a learned *scalar* to the attention logit; 32 log-spaced buckets per head up to offset 128, everything beyond mapped to one bucket; shared across layers.
buys: Nearly free in parameters: a scalar per bucket per head (the additive n×n bias still costs compute — ~2× slower training in Press et al.'s fairseq run, ~9% on TPU per Narang et al.)
Depends only on i−j, so KV-cache friendly
Deeper layers 'build sensitivity to larger offsets'
costs: Content-independent: cannot express content–position interactions the way Shaw / RoPE do
Beyond 128 every offset looks identical — a soft ceiling on precise long-range position
Weaker extrapolation than ALiBi (Press et al. 2021), though better than RoPE and sinusoidal; and the additive bias breaks the plain fast-attention path

rag32k.why: runs at 32K, but offsets past 128 share one bucket and the bias slows kernels

coding128k.why: everything beyond offset 128 is one bucket — no precise far position for cross-file recall

agent1m.why: an additive n×n bias off the fast path at 1M; all far offsets one bucket

pickWhen.verdict: The parameter-light relative scheme of the encoder-decoder world; decoders went RoPE. Note the co-author: Shazeer wrote MQA two weeks later.

name: Multi-Query Attention (MQA)

source.title: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need

secondary.label: AlphaCode — first mainstream use ('we take advantage of multi-query attention (Shazeer 2019)')

firstShipped.model: AlphaCode (DeepMind) — not PaLM, as often stated

problem: Nobody else in 2019 was looking at this bill: at incremental decoding each new token must re-read the whole cached K and V (n·d per layer), so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth, not FLOPs. The paper's ratio: Θ(n/d + 1/b).
idea: Keep h query heads but a single shared key head and value head. The KV cache and per-step memory traffic shrink by a factor h; the cost ratio becomes Θ(1/d + n/(dh) + 1/b).
buys: KV cache ÷ h; decoder incremental time 3.8 µs/token vs 46 µs/token (~12×) in the paper
Quality nearly intact: WMT14 En-De 28.5 vs 28.4 BLEU, dev log-ppl 1.439 vs 1.424
Enables large-batch, long-context serving — AlphaCode's sampling went 0.37 → 4.74 samples/TPU-s
costs: A small but real quality drop, and later work found MQA more prone to instability at scale — the reason GQA exists
No training-compute saving; must be chosen at pretraining time (or 'uptrained' à la GQA)
One KV head interacts badly with tensor parallelism — every shard needs the same K/V (Falcon-40B used per-shard KV, i.e. effectively grouped)

chatbot2k.why: little benefit when compute, not bandwidth, dominates

rag32k.why: KV bandwidth is the decode cost

agent1m.why: though GQA-8 or MLA is the usual modern choice at frontier scale

pickWhen.verdict: The first mechanism to see the KV bill, two years before anyone needed it. Today: small/edge models pick MQA; large ones pick GQA.

name: Explicit Sparse Transformer — top-k attention
aka: explicit selection; originally 'Sparse Transformer: Concentrated Attention Through Explicit Selection'

source.title: Explicit Sparse Transformer: Concentrated Attention Through Explicit Selection
source.authors: Zhao, Lin, Zhang, Ren, Su, Sun (Peking University)
source.evidence: [v1] Wed, 25 Dec 2019 10:59:31 UTC; public earlier as an ICLR 2020 OpenReview submission (25 Sep 2019)

secondary.label: Memory-efficient Transformers via Top-k Attention (Gupta et al.) — makes it chunked/efficient

firstShipped.model: Not in this form; top-k token selection reached production as DeepSeek Sparse Attention (V3.2-Exp)

problem: Softmax spreads mass over irrelevant tokens ('noise'). The original bill was quality — BLEU, CIDEr, perplexity — not compute: the full n×n matrix is still computed.
idea: Compute P = QKᵀ/√d, keep the k largest scores per row (k=8 worked best), set the rest to −∞, then softmax. No new parameters.
buys: Consistent gains over the baseline on En-De / En-Vi / De-En MT, MS-COCO captioning, enwik8
~2× faster than sparsemax and ~10× than α-entmax at inference (1.2× / 3.7× in training) because it is a plain mask
The conceptual seed of every 'attend to the k most relevant tokens' scheme (Quest, NSA select branch, DSA)
costs: No compute or memory saving in this form — the dense score matrix is computed and then masked
Hard selection has zero gradient to non-selected positions; k is a fixed hyperparameter, so a token needing broad context is capped
Efficient descendants had to pay for a cheap *indexer* (NSA, DSA) or chunked computation (Gupta 2021) to avoid the dense pre-pass

chatbot2k.why: as a regulariser on a small model, plausibly

coding128k.why: the dense 128K score matrix is still computed; a fixed k caps cross-file context

agent1m.why: only in its learned-indexer form (DSA), which is a different mechanism

pickWhen.verdict: Right idea, wrong decade: it needed a cheap way to *find* the top-k without computing everything, which arrived in 2025.

name: Reformer — LSH attention (+ reversible layers)

source.title: Reformer: The Efficient Transformer
source.evidence: [v1] Mon, 13 Jan 2020 18:38:28 UTC (ICLR 2020; OpenReview submission Sep 2019)

problem: 64K–1M-token sequences on a single 16 GB accelerator: activation memory per layer and O(n²) attention.
idea: Share Q and K, hash them into buckets with random rotations, sort, and attend only within (adjacent) buckets — O(n log n); reversible residuals so activations for one layer are stored instead of N.
buys: O(n log n) attention; 'sequences of 1M words on 16 GB' (Google blog)
Reversible layers cut activation memory to ~1 layer
costs: Requires shared Q/K (a token must be masked from attending to itself; LSH is not applied to encoder–decoder attention), and per-step hashing/sorting makes incremental decoding awkward
Multi-round hashing adds sequential ops; hashing noise slows convergence; large constants — gains only past ~2K
LSH sort/bucket is awkward on GPUs; no mainstream LLM ever shipped it

chatbot2k.why: gains only past ~2K; hashing noise and shared Q/K for no saving

rag32k.why: exact 32K is cheap on FlashAttention; LSH buckets can miss the chunk and decode awkwardly

coding128k.why: per-step hash-and-sort decoding, shared Q/K, and bucket misses on cross-file recall

agent1m.why: KV memory, not activation memory, is today's bill

pickWhen.verdict: A memory trick for 2020 hardware. Content-based sparsity returns in 2025 with learned indexers, not hashes.

name: Routing Transformer — content-based sparse attention via online k-means

source.title: Efficient Content-Based Sparse Attention with Routing Transformers

problem: Sparse patterns fixed by position (local/strided) miss content; can the sparsity pattern depend on what the tokens *say*?
idea: Layer-norm queries and keys onto the unit ball, cluster them into k≈√n centroids by online spherical k-means, and let each query attend within its cluster: O(n^1.5·d).
buys: Data-dependent sparsity; SOTA on PG-19 (33.2 ppl) and best among comparable sparse / XL models on Wikitext-103 (15.8 vs 18.3) in 2020
Framed attention as approximate maximum-inner-product search — the DSA framing five years early
costs: Balanced clusters need sort/gather/scatter — hardware-unfriendly; tokens can land in several or no clusters
Centroid EMA maintenance; shared QK in causal mode
The authors note plain local attention is 'a surprisingly strong baseline'

chatbot2k.why: at 2K, sort/gather/scatter clustering costs more than the dense attention it replaces

rag32k.why: the query and its retrieved chunk can land in different clusters; sort/gather is hardware-unfriendly

coding128k.why: cross-file recall depends on landing in the right cluster; shared QK in causal mode

agent1m.why: the goal is right; today it is done with a learned top-k indexer (DSA), not k-means

pickWhen.verdict: The right question ('choose keys by content') answered with 2020 tools.

name: Sliding-window (+ dilated + global) attention — Longformer

secondary.label: Idea lineage: Luong local attention 2015; Image Transformer local blocks 2018; Sparse Transformer banded 2019
GPT-3 ships banded local layers (Sparse-Transformer lineage)
Mistral 7B — 'sliding window attention' in a mainstream open LLM, W=4096, rolling KV buffer

firstShipped.model: Mistral 7B (as 'SWA'; GPT-3's banded layers came earlier from the Sparse-Transformer line)

problem: BERT/RoBERTa stopped at 512 tokens because of quadratic memory; long-document QA, summarisation and coreference needed 4K–16K, ideally as a drop-in for a pretrained checkpoint.
idea: Each token attends to w/2 neighbours on each side — O(n·w) — with dilated windows on some heads and a few *global* tokens (task tokens, [CLS]) that attend everywhere; receptive field grows ℓ·w with depth.
buys: Linear in n; at w=512 the same per-query attention compute as RoBERTa on 4,096-token inputs (8× a 512-token pass, not the 64× dense would cost); beat RoBERTa on long-doc tasks
The KV cache is bounded by w — the reason Mistral 7B could keep a rolling buffer
The pattern the field settled on for the *cheap* layers of every 2024–25 hybrid (Gemma 2/3, gpt-oss, Command A)
costs: Windowed layers see only w tokens; long-range information must percolate through depth, and global tokens are needed to stay competitive

Banded matmul is not native: the naive loop is 'unusably slow'; the chunked PyTorch version (2× memory) is what the paper trained with; the custom TVM kernel was needed for dilation and the longest LM runs
No free length extrapolation — position still has to be handled — and pure sliding window everywhere hurts retrieval

rag32k.why: as the local layers of a local:global stack

coding128k.why: same; keep some dense/global layers for cross-file recall

agent1m.why: bounded KV is exactly what you want, but retrieval needs the global layers or a sparse indexer

pickWhen.verdict: Right as one half of a hybrid; wrong as the whole story for anything retrieval-heavy.

name: Linformer — low-rank projected keys/values

source.title: Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity
source.authors: Wang, Li, Khabsa, Fang, Ma (Facebook AI)

problem: The softmax attention matrix is empirically (and by the JL lemma, provably) low-rank; why compute all n² of it?
idea: Project K and V along the *sequence* axis with learned n×k matrices; attention becomes softmax(Q(EK)ᵀ)(FV) in O(nk).
buys: k=128–256 matched RoBERTa on GLUE at n=512/1024
1.5× (n=512) to 20× (n=65K) inference speedups reported
costs: The n×k projections bake a maximum length into the weights — no extrapolation, must pad
Mixing all positions breaks causal masking: bidirectional only, never for decoding
Low-rank fails when attention must be sharp / pointer-like

rag32k.why: bidirectional only, and low rank fails at the sharp pointer-like attention retrieval needs

coding128k.why: never for decoding; length baked into the n×k projection; cross-file recall needs sharp attention

agent1m.why: no decoding at all; a 1M×k projection baked into weights — MLA compresses features instead

pickWhen.verdict: Fixed-length encoders only. The low-rank instinct returns, done differently, as MLA's latent KV in 2024 — MLA compresses each token along the feature axis (stays causal); Linformer compresses along the sequence axis, which is what breaks decoding.

name: Linear attention — 'Transformers are RNNs'
aka: Linear Transformer; kernelised attention; feature-map (elu+1) attention

source.title: Transformers are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Transformers with Linear Attention

secondary.label: Earlier: Performer/FAVOR protein paper (random features, no causal RNN form)
Earlier still: Efficient Attention (Shen et al.), vision, linear complexity

firstShipped.model: MiniMax-01 — the first frontier-scale hybrid (RWKV-4 in Aug 2022 and RetNet in 2023 shipped the family earlier at open/research scale)

problem: Two bills at once: O(n²) attention, and autoregressive inference whose per-token cost *and memory* grow with context — the paper stresses that Sparse Transformer and Reformer 'do not speed up autoregressive inference'.
idea: Replace exp(q·k) with φ(q)ᵀφ(k), φ = elu+1. Associativity gives φ(Q)(φ(K)ᵀV) in O(n). In the causal case this is an RNN with a d×d state S = Σ φ(k_j)v_jᵀ and a normaliser z — constant per-token cost and constant memory, no KV cache at all.
buys: O(n) time and memory; constant-cost decoding with a fixed-size state instead of a growing KV cache
Up to 4,000× faster CIFAR-10 image generation vs the paper's non-caching softmax baseline (~50× vs a KV-cached softmax, per its own appendix); comparable bits/dim
The template every 2023–25 linear layer (RetNet, GLA, DeltaNet, lightning attention) builds on
costs: Not softmax: elu+1 is a weak kernel; a real quality gap where sharp attention matters (WSJ ASR PER 8.08 vs 5.12)
A fixed d×d state bounds what can be remembered — the recall/retrieval weakness the delta rule later attacks
Causal training via cumulative sums is bandwidth-bound and needs custom kernels; pure linear attention has never matched softmax at frontier scale — production uses hybrids

chatbot2k.why: exact recall at 2K is cheap; do not give it up

rag32k.why: as the cheap layers of a hybrid; not for the retrieval layers

agent1m.why: constant per-token memory is the whole point at 1M — in a 3:1 / 7:1 hybrid

pickWhen.verdict: It buys a bounded state and sells exact recall. Right when the sequence is long and the memory bill is binding; wrong when you need to find one needle.

name: BigBird — window + global + random block-sparse attention

source.title: Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences

problem: Get BERT-style encoders to 4,096 tokens (8×) on the same hardware, with theory that sparse attention keeps expressivity (universal approximation, Turing completeness).
idea: On 64-token blocks: a sliding window (3 blocks) + a few global tokens + 3 random blocks per query, so window/global reduce to dense block matmuls.
buys: 8× longer encoder inputs; SOTA long-doc QA and summarisation in 2020
Theory: sparse attention with global tokens is as expressive as full
costs: Random attention needs gathers the paper itself calls inefficient
Global tokens are essential ('random blocks and local window were insufficient') — a hint at attention sinks
Encoder-only; never in a mainstream decoder LLM

chatbot2k.why: dense at 2K beats random-block gathers the paper itself calls inefficient

rag32k.why: long-doc encoders with a RoBERTa/Pegasus checkpoint

coding128k.why: encoder-only; random blocks plus gathers give no reliable cross-file recall path in a decoder

agent1m.why: never in a mainstream decoder; random-block gathers at 1M and no KV story

pickWhen.verdict: The most complete 2020 pattern; too fiddly and too encoder-shaped to survive into decoders.

name: Performer — FAVOR+ random-feature softmax

source.title: Rethinking Attention with Performers
source.authors: Choromanski et al. (Google / Cambridge / DeepMind / Alan Turing Inst.)
source.evidence: [v1] Wed, 30 Sep 2020 17:09:09 UTC (ICLR 2021); FAVOR without '+' in 2006.03555, 5 Jun 2020

problem: Linear attention with an arbitrary kernel is not softmax. Can we approximate the *actual* softmax kernel, unbiased, at linear cost — so pretrained models convert?
idea: exp(q·k) as an expectation over positive orthogonal random features; m = Θ(d log d) features independent of n; then φ(Q)(φ(K)ᵀV).
buys: Provably unbiased, linear-cost softmax surrogate
Competitive on protein LM, ImageNet-64, PG-19
costs: Approximation error compounds through layers — pretrained weights still need fine-tuning
sin/cos features NaN; positive features mandatory and must be redrawn
Variance for peaked attention; not competitive with exact softmax on LM at scale; never shipped

chatbot2k.why: exact softmax at 2K is cheap; random features add approximation error for no gain

rag32k.why: variance for peaked attention — the sharp pointer retrieval needs is what FAVOR+ approximates worst

coding128k.why: error compounds through layers and peaked far-token attention has the highest variance — recall suffers

agent1m.why: right bill, wrong kernel: 1M linear layers use delta-rule/GLA states, not random features

pickWhen.verdict: Elegant theory, and the last serious attempt to be softmax without paying for softmax. FlashAttention made the question moot for a while.

name: QK-Norm (query-key normalisation)

secondary.label: Gemma 3: 'we replace the soft-capping of Gemma 2 with QK-norm'

firstShipped.model: ViT-22B (vision); in LLMs Chameleon (May 2024), OLMoE (Sep 2024), OLMo 2, Gemma 3, Qwen3

problem: The 2020 paper: softmax saturation limits diffuse attention in low-resource MT (+0.93 BLEU). The loss-spikes-at-scale motivation — logits growing without bound at high LR or long context — comes from ViT-22B (2023) and Wortsman et al., which is where LLM recipes took it from.
idea: Normalise q and k per head (L2 or RMSNorm) before the dot product; add a learnable scale so the temperature is not fixed.
buys: Bounded logits, stable large-scale training, higher LR; Gemma 3 dropped logit soft-capping for it
costs: Extra norms per head (small); fixes the temperature so a scale must be learned; interacts with fused-QK kernels and with attention sinks

rag32k.why: bounded logits regardless of length, for one extra per-head norm

coding128k.why: logits growing with context length is the ViT-22B failure it bounds

agent1m.why: the longer the context, the more logits drift; bounded logits are non-negotiable at 1M

pickWhen.verdict: Not a bill item — a stability item — but you cannot read a 2025 attention block without it.

name: Adaptive Attention Span
oneLiner: Each head learns its own soft attention span, so most heads stay local and a few reach far — a learned sliding window a year before Longformer.
whyFootnote: Same family as sliding window; not separately adopted.

name: Sparse Sinkhorn Attention
oneLiner: Learns a differentiable block permutation (Sinkhorn balancing) so local attention over re-sorted blocks approximates content-based sparsity.
whyFootnote: One of several 2020 content-sparse designs; not adopted.

name: Talking-Heads Attention
oneLiner: Linear projections across the heads dimension before and after softmax — more quality for more compute.
whyFootnote: Moves the bill the wrong way; a quality tweak, not an efficiency mechanism.

name: ETC — Extended Transformer Construction

source.title: ETC: Encoding Long and Structured Inputs in Transformers

oneLiner: Global–local attention with a separate global memory; BigBird is 'an extension over ETC'. Same first author as GQA three years later.
whyFootnote: Subsumed by Longformer/BigBird on the timeline.

name: Fast Transformers with Clustered Attention
oneLiner: Cluster queries, compute attention once per centroid, broadcast — from the same group as linear attention ten days earlier.

name: Long Range Arena (benchmark)

source.title: Long Range Arena: A Benchmark for Efficient Transformers

oneLiner: The benchmark that lined up Reformer, Linformer, Linear Transformer, Longformer, BigBird, Performer, Sinkhorn and found no clear winner — and, in hindsight, did not predict what would ship.
whyFootnote: A benchmark, not a mechanism; included because it closes the 2020 wave.
